h.strategy: Naive reasoning predicts substitution: if something similar exists elsewhere, an edit helps less. Experts find this obvious, so at most two hypotheses may use it. At least three hypotheses must predict the opposite, complementarity, where an edit helps MORE because a different kind of component elsewhere supplies what it lacks. At least two must predict a reversal, where a usually beneficial edit becomes harmful under a specific condition through trainability, merged-signal scale, or over-capacity. Never condition on the edited field's own value or on settings that make the edit inert. Each hypothesis must couple two different fields, and no condition setting may appear more than twice. In each 'why', give the mechanism in two or three sentences, state why an expert might bet the other way, and name the refuting comparison. The critic should replace any hypothesis that duplicates another's mechanism.

hyps.why: Replacing none with skip adds a direct input-to-output path, a larger gain than replacing an existing conv or pool with skip, which can even hurt.
Adding a conv where node 2 had no output path creates a new learned route, worth more than upgrading an existing op.
A strong 3x3 conv already feeds node 3 directly, so an extra 1x1 conv adds less than when edge 3 is weak.
Skip replacing none opens a new path into node 2, whereas skip replacing a conv removes learned capacity.
With a 3x3 conv already feeding node 3 from node 1, another 3x3 on edge 5 gives diminishing returns.
If edge 0 is none, node 1 carries no signal so edge 2 is inert and upgrading it does almost nothing.
If edge 0 is none, node 1 is dead so a conv on edge 4 has nothing to process.
Replacing none with a conv adds a whole direct path, worth more than upgrading an existing skip or pool.
Adding a conv where the edge was absent creates a new learned path through node 1, a bigger gain than upgrading an existing op.
Turning an absent edge into a 3x3 conv opens a new learned branch into node 2, a larger gain than upgrading an existing op.
